name: Germany
governanceModel: EU AI Act implemented nationally via the new KI-MIG enforcement law
debateTopics: CEO personal liability under the KI-MIG enforcement law
Germany's sovereign AI champion changes hands
overview:
Germany passed its own AI Act enforcement legislation in mid-2026 — the KI-MIG (AI Act Implementing Act), approved by the Bundestag on 11 June, naming the Bundesnetzagentur as market-surveillance authority and introducing personal liability for company executives over AI security failures from 2 August 2026, with fines of up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover. Dr. Karsten Wildberger has led the restructured Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernisation (BMDS) as Germany's first-ever Digital Minister since May 2025.

2026's other defining German AI story was industrial rather than regulatory: Aleph Alpha, long framed as the country's sovereign answer to OpenAI and Mistral, agreed to be acquired by Canada's Cohere — a striking juxtaposition alongside the new Germany-Canada Sovereign Technology Alliance.

debates.topic: CEO personal liability under the KI-MIG enforcement law
debates.summary: Germany's new AI Act implementing law introduces personal liability for executives over AI security failures — a sharper enforcement edge than most peer EU states have adopted nationally.
debates.expanded: From 2 August 2026, company executives can be held personally liable for AI security failures under KI-MIG, alongside fines of up to €35M or 7% of global turnover. Industry groups warn this could push some AI deployment decisions toward excessive caution or offshore structuring; the government frames it as necessary teeth for a law that would otherwise be difficult to enforce against large multinational deployers.

debates.topic: Germany's sovereign AI champion changes hands
debates.summary: Aleph Alpha's acquisition by Canada's Cohere raises the question of what 'sovereign AI' means when a national champion is sold to a foreign lab.
debates.expanded: Aleph Alpha had been positioned for years as Germany's answer to dependence on US and French AI labs. Its 2026 acquisition by Cohere — itself the subject of a new Germany-Canada tech alliance — complicates the sovereignty narrative: German enterprise and public-sector AI (like the Federal Employment Agency's helpdesk) now runs on technology owned by a foreign company, even if a friendly one.

debates.summary: A new alliance with Canada aims to reduce both countries' strategic technology dependency — launched in the same period as Canada's Cohere acquired Germany's own flagship AI lab.
debates.expanded: The alliance's stated aim is deepening cooperation on sovereign technology capability between the two countries. Its practical meaning is still being worked out, particularly given the Aleph Alpha acquisition running in parallel.
